newsitem.title: BELGIUM: EU seeks united front to narrow wealth gap.
newsitem.headline: EU seeks united front to narrow wealth gap.

text.p: European Commissioners sought on Monday to hide deep divisions and forge a united front in the battle to narrow a wide gap in living standards between rich and poor EU members and prepare for expansion eastwards.

During a three-day conference to discuss reforms to EU regional, social and farm aid spending, 1200 experts from the EU's 15 member states and 10 east European applicant countries will discuss a strategy for a massive new seven-year spending programme starting in 1999.

"We are still a long way from our grand goal of creating a single European area which is competitive, regionally well-balanced and firmly anchored in its social dimension," EU Regional Affairs Commissioner Monika Wulf-Mathies said in a speech.

The EU has failed to bridge the poverty gap despite spending 170 billion ecus ($192 billion) between 1994-99 to help the poorer countries -- Portugal, Greece, Ireland and Spain -- catch up with their richer partners.
The EU's Irish social affairs commissioner Padraig Flynn deplored that so much money had been spent to so little effect.
Despite an overall increase in wealth over the past 10 years, "...the shaming fact is that poverty in our societies has actually increased," Flynn said in a speech.
"Although unemployment is now on the way down, it still blights one in 10 of our total potential workforce," he added.
Flynn noted that the EU jobless rate was double that of the United States and triple that of Japan.
The EU's Austrian farm commissioner Franz Fischler noted that the regions which most depend on agriculture also suffered the highest unemployment rates and lowest earnings per worker.
The EU was in need of a more integrated approach to rural development, he said, explaining that economic, social, educational, agricultural and environmental policy should be brought together.
"(It) will help open up new prospects for rural areas and activate local potential," Fischler said.
Fischler also said that concentration of aid on particular topics, rather than geographical areas, was more likely to achieve sustainable rural development.
Around a quarter of EU citizens live in rural areas, ranging from the olive groves of Spain to the frozen tundra of northern Finland, covering 80 percent of EU territory.
But Fischler's blueprint, launched last November in Cork, Ireland, to combine farm and regional rural aid programme, has provoked strong opposition from farmers' friends and foes alike.

Farmers feared it would drain farm aid into rural tourism, crafts and other industries. But Wulf-Mathies is concerned it would allow a minority of wealthy farmers, who already grab 80 percent of EU farm funds, access to even more cash.
